Program „Zdrava hrana svakog dana“ ove školske godine nastavlja edukacije učenika četvrtog razreda u osnovnim školama širom Srbije
Interaktivna predavanja nutricioniste za učenike četvrtog razreda, koja su do sada održana u 337 osnovnih škola, od ovog septembra stižu u nove učionice širom Srbije.
Kroz zanimljive razgovore o pravilnoj i uravnoteženoj ishrani, učenici u okviru Maxi programa edukacije „Zdrava hrana svakog dana“ uče o tome zašto je važno da se doručak ne preskače, povrće nađe u svakom obroku, voće bira za užinu, a hidratacija i fizička aktivnost budu neizostavan deo svakodnevice.
Program edukacije, kroz koji je do sada prošlo više od 30.000 učenika četvrtih razreda, ove školske godine obići će osnovne škole u Sremskoj Mitrovici, Rumi, Inđiji, Pančevu, Vršcu, Zrenjaninu i Kovinu.
Programu „Zdrava hrana svakog dana“ prvi su ove godine prisustvovali četvrtaci Osnovne škole „Jovan Jovanović Zmaj“ iz Sremske Mitrovice.
Oni su u razgovoru sa nutricionistkinjom Ivanom Mišić podelili svoje dileme oko školske užine i zdravog doručka, ali i razgovarali o tome koliko je fizičke aktivnosti važno imati tokom nedelje.
„Veoma nam je drago što se naša škola našla u programu ’Zdrava hrana svakog dana’. Tema zdrave ishrane i pravilnog razvoja dece izuzetno je važna, a naši nastavnici se trude da u radu sa decom, uz redovan nastavni plan i program, što više pažnje posvećuju i ovim pitanjima.
Zato se radujemo svakoj dodatnoj inicijativi koja decu edukuje i podstiče ih da razmišljaju o zdravijim izborima i navikama. Škola nije samo mesto gde se uče lekcije i dobijaju ocene, već i sredina u kojoj se oblikuju navike koje deca nose sa sobom kroz život.
Verujem da ovakva predavanja mogu da budu važan podsticaj da ono što danas nauče sutra postane deo njihove svakodnevice“, istakla je Sonja Tucaković, direktorka OŠ „Jovan Jovanović Zmaj“.
Maxi karavan „Zdrava hrana svakog dana“ pokrenut je 2023. godine uz podršku Ministarstva prosvete, a ove školske godine ušao je u četvrtu godinu redovnih edukacija đaka u školama širom Srbije.
„Do sada smo obišli škole u oko 70 gradova, opština i naselja, i svaki susret sa decom za nas je posebno inspirativan. Energija i entuzijazam četvrtaka u Sremskoj Mitrovici još jednom su nam pokazali koliko je važno da o ovim temama razgovaramo sa učenicima.
Zdrave navike u ishrani i ljubav prema sportu svoje osnove grade još u detinjstvu. Zato ćemo i ove školske godine sa puno radosti biti sa učenicima u fiskulturnim salama i učionicama, razgovarati o zdravim navikama i zajedno učiti kako da ih gradimo i negujemo, dok ćemo njihove ideje i iskustva koristiti da ovaj program iz godine u godinu učinimo još boljim“, rekla je Milica Rakovac, ispred trgovinskog lanca Maxi.

title: 10 Jahre Ausbildungspflicht - 36.000 Jugendliche begleitet
content:
Wien – Seit dem Ende des Schuljahres 2016/17 gilt die Ausbildungspflicht für Jugendliche bis 18. Wer seither seine Schulpflicht erfüllt hat, muss anschließend bis zur Vollendung des 18. Lebensjahrs entweder eine weiterführende Schule besuchen oder eine andere Ausbildung machen. Bisher wurden 36.000 Jugendliche begleitet, die gegen die Pflicht zunächst verstießen, so Sozialministerin Korinna Schumann (SPÖ) am Freitag. 86 Prozent der Begleitungen wurden positiv abgeschlossen.

title: April Laguros came from the Philippines to save a regional aged care facility
content:
April Laguros left her family in the Philippines to live in Coolamon
When April Laguros contemplated leaving behind her husband and three young kids in the Philippines to come to Australia, it wasn't iconic coastline she saw when she googled her future home — it was canola.
"I searched about Coolamon … What does it look like? And I can see the yellow fields, golden fields".
When April arrived in the small agricultural town, 30 minutes north-west of Wagga Wagga, with 14 other new immigrants, they found themselves in a foreign landscape. The canola fields weren't even in bloom.
"It looked like desert for me," she said. She thought: "What kind of place are we going through?"
Cebu, April's original home, is a bustling coastal city with a population close to a million people. Coolamon in New South Wales has a population closer to 2,000. Fifteen new faces did not go unnoticed.
"Obviously this is a rural community, you know, where the town is predominantly white, Anglo-Saxon, farming," says Melanie Stubbs, the human resources officer at Coolamon Shire Council.
"And so, to have such a big group arrive … it was quite a surprise, and it was a learning curve for the community."
Coolamon's problem and April's sacrifice
April came seeking opportunity for herself and her family, but it came at a price.
"It was lonely, sad, but I just hold on to the reason why I came here. The reason is for my family … because I have to bring my kids here. I have to save and then bring them and then experience a good life here in Australia," she says.
Tony Donoghue, Coolamon Shire Council general manager, was moved when he learnt April had left such young kids at home.
"I thought, 'Oh my God, how did you do that?' But … living in Australia is her goal and that's our goal as well," he says.
For Coolamon Shire Council, April and her new colleagues were a desperately needed life raft for the local residential aged care facility.
Allawah Lodge is council-run, with capacity for 33 residents, but not enough local staff to operate at full capacity.
"The risk was closing and I didn't think that was appropriate," says Tony.
"We believe in our community that we should look after our elderly and we didn't want to have our most respected community members scattered around across the region in various nursing homes."
The solution was to sponsor 15 immigrant workers; no small feat for a regional local council.
"We had to build a home for the Filipino community because there was no accommodation here. So this council invested $750,000 in just that building alone," says Tony.
April says she felt welcome and supported by the community.
"When we came here in Coolamon they knew already that we are the Filipinos that will be working in Allawah Lodge …they welcomed us warmly," says April.
Over breakfast, the Allawah Lodge residents sing the Filipino staff's praises.
Long term Coolamon resident Barb says: "Oh, [we] love them to bits. We get cuddles and hugs and dances and singing and most of all terrific care."
"When they bring the food. I can say 'salamat', which means thank you," says another resident, George.
But around the corner at Coolamon Shire Hall, Melanie from the council acknowledges it hasn't all been smooth sailing.
"There was one day I was helping all of the staff open a bank account and a gentleman who is a very long-standing community member, he's since passed away, but you know, born and bred here.
"And he scooted along on his scooter, and he asked them all if they spoke English and then very quickly told them all that they were not welcome in his home," Melanie recalls.
"That particular gentleman ended up being a resident in our aged care facility. And those staff … cared for him like anyone else, which was really beautiful. Really beautiful."
April says while she hasn't experienced racism in the Coolamon community, she has at Allawah Lodge.
"We have one resident who is racist, but we just think that she has dementia and she doesn't know what she's talking about," says April.
One of her Filipino colleagues at Allawah Lodge, Jeffrey, says this is part and parcel with aged care work.
"It is awful to say that you get used to it, but it comes with the trade".
Another Filipino staff member, Nova, says she tries not to take it personally.
"Sometimes you feel hurt and then you can just move away and then come back again because … they need us," she says.
April's family reunited in Coolamon
More than two years after April arrived in Australia, she yells "who wants ice-cream?" across a Coolamon park. It's her day off and she's watching her kids, aged three, five and 13, climb together on the equipment.
"I was very happy when I brought them here and, on that day, I am very grateful … realising that I can provide a good life for them [in Australia]," she says.
Her husband has come too and has a local job as a welder.
When council general manager Tony Donoghue reflects on April's journey, he tears up.
"It's making me a little bit emotional … We've made a difference to people".
"I think our regions are fantastic places to live," he says.
"I think that's something that I'd love the city folk to understand. It's great to live here".
Just outside town, the Canola fields are in full bloom for spring.

title: New experiential festival brings racial and religious harmony to life for youth
content:
New experiential festival brings racial and religious harmony to life for youth
- The #commUNITY on Campus festival at SMU celebrates racial and religious harmony by showcasing scents, tastes, and cultural objects from diverse faiths to build cross-cultural understanding among youths.
- Organised by Youth Leaders @ Harmony Circle and supported by the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth, the festival offers hands-on experiences and highlights similarities across religions, such as shared incense rituals.
- The event aims to prepare young people for a diverse workforce by deepening their appreciation of multiracial and multireligious Singapore, emphasising the ongoing importance of harmony in society.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – Despite being Buddhist, undergraduates Evlin Woo and Chloe Chua did not know the origins of the familiar scents that form part of their religious heritage.
At a festival celebrating racial and religious harmony held at Singapore Management University on Sept 18, they got up close and personal with Bodhi leaves, mani pills and joss sticks made from sandalwood and agarwood.
These items were featured at experiential booths meant to help young people understand different cultures and beliefs.
The event was jointly developed by 80 young people from Youth Leaders @ Harmony Circle (YLHC) and 15 student cultural, faith-based and interfaith clubs across four institutes of higher learning (IHLs) and other youth groups.
The #commUNITY on Campus festival, led by YLHC and supported by the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth, will be held every two years at a different IHL.
On Sept 18, more than 600 attendees became acquainted with the tastes and scents of different cultures.
Chua, who studies accountancy, said: “A lot of the scents were familiar, but I think we never heard of the origin.”
In addition to the different tastes and aromas from different cultures, attendees also got to touch objects such as prayer beads, sacred threads and cloths.
Woo and Chua said they also learnt about the different objects associated with the Judaic faith, such as tefillin – two black leather boxes with straps traditionally worn by men each weekday morning before prayer – and tallit, a fringed prayer shawl.
“(Representatives at the Judaism booth) also shared information about their culture and their beliefs and how they don’t use their phones or any devices on Saturday. It was nice to hear that this practice is part of their culture,” said Chua.
Software engineer Fathima Raeesah learnt that Taoism and Hinduism share common beliefs when it comes to incense. Both religions believe that rising incense smoke represents the ascension of prayer.
“I was able to see how the different religions have a lot of similarities between different aspects such as their flavours and scents. Learning about the differences is also a way to embrace the similarities they share,” said the 25-year-old.
Derek Tan, who co-led the organising committee of the festival, said the event brings different cultures and traditions together in a more relaxed and engaging way, which is useful as people may not always have the opportunity to have conversations across communities.
The other co-lead of the organising committee, Ismail Meera Begum, said the experiential booths let attendees understand first-hand the common ground between different cultures.
For example, talbina, a traditional food rooted in Islamic history and recommended by Prophet Muhammad, is similar to tea in the Sikh tradition in that they are both symbols of hospitality.
“This festival gives people insight into the meaning behind certain food and beverages. They may not realise there is actually a deeper meaning behind such traditional food,” said Meera.
She added that the festival is catered to youth because when they enter the workforce, they will encounter a world that is different from school.
“Racial and religious harmony is a very important aspect which we need to cultivate in young people so that when they face the world, they know what to expect and how to handle certain differences that may come about.”
Speaking at the festival, Senior Parliamentary Secretary for Culture, Community and Youth Goh Hanyan said Singapore cannot take racial and religious harmony for granted.
She said: “For the younger generation, you all have a very different perspective, probably, of what it means to be a multiracial, multi-religious society in Singapore.
“I’m very happy that you have taken interest in such an important theme... and... try to update this unique brand that we have in Singapore of being multiracial and multi-religious.”

title: How students are picking vocational and trade subjects to boost their ATAR
content:
How students are picking vocational and trade subjects to boost their ATAR
Tanya Bolt said when her eldest son, Seth, chose his senior subjects at the end of year 10, university was not something on his mind.
Less than a year later, as the 16-year-old began showing an interest in university courses, Bolt said picking vocational subjects was the best decision he could have made.
“Chatting with his English teacher, she said, ‘It breaks my heart because it actually gives a higher ATAR than had he gone for a [standard] ATAR pathway at school’,” Bolt said.
The Gold Coast year 11 student opted to pursue a diploma in business as a vocational education and training (VET) subject, but remained eligible for an ATAR – universities’ key criterion for student selection into tertiary courses.
In Queensland, senior students studying vocational subjects can receive an ATAR provided they meet minimum maths and English requirements, complete their VET qualification before graduating, and study four general subjects at a year 12 level.
When these requirements are met, the Queensland Tertiary Admissions Centre (QTAC) converts vocational subjects – graded on an A-to-E scale – into a score out of 100 that can be included in students’ ATAR calculations.
Bolt said pursuing a standard ATAR pathway of six general subjects across year 11 and 12 would have been “a waste of time” for Seth.
“Sitting in economics, sitting in psychology, sitting in woodwork – he just had no interest whatsoever,” she said.
Instead, Bolt said her son was keen to follow his father into property development, although he had also considered a sports coaching business or, more recently, studying town planning at university.
However, in Seth’s case, Bolt said the 16-year-old would likely walk “straight in” to university with his diploma alone.
QTAC chief executive Chris Veraa said many Queensland universities often considered external qualifications above a certificate IV level – the step below a diploma – on their own.
“Traditionally, universities have assessed VET qualifications by assigning them a selection rank or ATAR equivalent to determine an applicant’s competitiveness for entry,” he said.
At Brisbane universities Queensland University of Technology and University of Queensland, a completed VET diploma could be considered equivalent to an ATAR up to 87 and 82, respectively.
For a certificate IV, the same universities translated a passing grade into a rank up to 72.
At Griffith University, certain courses guaranteed entry to students who had completed VET qualifications equal or higher than a certificate III – including the urban planning degree Seth was considering.
The tertiary admissions centre found the number of university applicants using VET scores – either directly or indirectly – grew by 18 per cent in the past two years.
Veraa said universities were increasingly offering guaranteed and direct admissions pathways based on VET qualifications, with direct entries growing by 21.2 per cent since 2024.
“This reflects a broader shift in how VET is being used within tertiary pathways, with applicants increasingly considering VET as either an input to, or an alternative pathway into, higher education,” he said.

title: Flash floods can strike without warning — this new technology could change that
content:
On the morning of June 9th, Laura Lin was working from her home in Lanesville, a rural southern Indiana town about 15 miles from the Kentucky border. She was on a Zoom call, unaware that the heavy rain outside was beginning to flood her yard.
Flash floods can strike without warning — this new technology could change that
Satellite data combined with machine learning gives meteorologists new tools to predict deadly floods sooner.
Flash floods can strike without warning — this new technology could change that
Satellite data combined with machine learning gives meteorologists new tools to predict deadly floods sooner.
“I look over to where the barn is over there, and I see pieces of my wood floating, and I was like, ‘What?’ And I immediately was like, ‘I have to go.’ Close my laptop, and I get my kids up, and I’m like, ‘Something’s wrong,’” Lin recalls.
Lin and her family got out safely and sheltered at a neighbor’s house, but Lanesville got over 8 inches of rain within just a few hours that day, way over the threshold for what is considered “heavy” rainfall. The water was gone a few hours later.
Floods are the second-deadliest type of weather event in the United States and the deadliest globally. Just 6 inches of fast-flowing water can knock an adult off their feet, 12 inches can lift a car, and 2 feet can move larger vehicles like trucks and SUVs. A warming climate means more instances of extreme rainfall in the US, creating more opportunities for floods to occur. The deadly flash flooding in Nepal in August caused by a glacier collapse shows the power of water to devastate communities worldwide.
Fortunately, new tools are being developed to counter this threat. A new software called the Transient Artifact and Continuous Learning System (TACLS) uses satellites and machine learning to try to spot areas that could flood sooner and help the National Weather Service (NWS) make better decisions when it comes to issuing flash flood alerts.
“We didn’t get the ‘get on your roof’ warnings until I was already at that person’s house,” Lin says. “All the people in town were already flooded when they started sending out alerts, being like, ‘Get on your roof. We’re dispatching boats.’ So it was way too late.”
TACLS has the potential to help change that.
“It will help you save lives,” says Ivory Small, science and operations officer at the NWS San Diego Weather Forecast Office. Without TACLS, Small says, a storm moving into your area “could kill some folks.” With TACLS, “you can put out the warning and save some folks.”
Follow the water
Weather forecast offices are responsible for issuing severe weather alerts, including flash flood warnings. There are 122 of them throughout the US and its territories, says Jayme Laber, senior service hydrologist for the NWS Weather Forecast Office in Oxnard, California, which oversees the LA area. Small and Laber worked closely on the TACLS project with a broader team of scientists and researchers, and they hope this new project will streamline weather alerts. To understand TACLS, it’s important to first understand how the NWS issues flood alerts.
Currently, the people working in weather forecast offices use a variety of tools to monitor flood conditions. They rely on rain and stream gauges to tell them how much water is in a certain place at any given time, Laber says. They track developing storms using satellites and weather radars. The staff monitors rainfall, but their computers also alert them when it rains more than what is considered safe for a specific area. “Based on the type of soils we have, the steepness of slopes, we have developed flash flood guidance so that we know that if we get this amount of rain in this amount of time in that area, it could result in flash flooding,” Laber says.
“It will help you save lives.”
— Ivory SmallAll of that, plus the years of expertise inside those buildings, determines whether or not someone presses a button to issue a flood alert for their area, Laber says.
A watch is the least serious alert. It means that there’s a chance a flash flood could happen. The watch might be issued anywhere from 12 to 48 hours in advance, Laber explains. He says local emergency teams should start working on “flood protection measures” when the flood watch is issued, so there’s enough time to prepare before people are stuck and forced to find higher ground. Response teams might review evacuation plans, set up sandbags and road barriers, and identify the highest risk areas ahead of a potential flood.
An advisory is the next level up. It might be flooding, “but it’s more nuisance-level. It’s not going to threaten life or property,” Laber says. A warning is the most serious alert. “That’s a life-and-death possibility of being swept off your feet [or] being run over by a car floating down the stream,” Small says.
The NWS differentiates a regular flood from a flash flood based on time, says Small. If an area floods in under six hours, it’s a flash flood.
The NWS has a lot of different ways to determine whether or not it needs to issue a flash flood warning, but its tech has limitations, says Yehuda Bock, TACLS project lead and research geodesist at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California, San Diego. The satellites the NWS uses are more detailed over oceans than land, he says. And tracking rainfall as it’s happening doesn’t give you enough lead time, “because once there’s precipitation, you’re already in the event itself,” he explains.
Deserts and other less populated areas typically have fewer rain gauges, Laber says. “We have a fairly dense network [of rain gauges], but it doesn’t cover every inch of the Earth.”
Up in the air
TACLS uses satellites and machine learning to identify places on a map — for now, just in California — that risk transitioning from rain to dangerous flash floods. But soon, the technology will be available to every NWS office. Scientists from UCSD, the NWS, and NASA worked together to create TACLS. NASA’s Earth Science Technology Office funded the project through its Advanced Information Systems Technology program.
TACLS relies on the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS), which is primarily used to predict earthquakes, says Bock. But the GNSS network, which consists of satellites and ground sensors, also happens to provide data that can help forecasters decide if they need to issue a flash flood warning. The more water vapor, or moisture, there is in the atmosphere, the longer the delay in communication between the GNSS satellites and the sensors on the ground.
The amount of moisture, or “precipitable water,” in the atmosphere tells the NWS what is actually happening in the skies leading up to a storm, Laber says.
TACLS uses satellites and machine learning to identify places that risk transitioning from rain to dangerous flash floods.
Before TACLS, Laber and his colleagues had to rely on the forecast, which wasn’t always accurate. TACLS provides real-time data about the precipitable water in the atmosphere to compare to the forecast. This helps them determine whether the storm is actually moving at the speed predicted by the weather models. “It helps us to make better decisions in our warning decision process,” Laber says.
Even with the GNSS moisture data, forecasters still need something to analyze all of it. Bhavik Chandna, a UCSD graduate student, spent about a year developing the machine learning side of TACLS using what’s called long short-term memory architecture. According to Chandna, this specific machine learning system works especially well for things like developing storms and other weather patterns that change over time.
Years of atmospheric measurements from the GNSS network, as well as data about atmospheric rivers, precipitation, and flash flood warnings, were used to train the machine learning model to understand moisture changes in the atmosphere “as a storm develops,” Chandna explains. At the same time, the machine learning system was trained to determine if the conditions are right to issue a flash flood warning.
“Machine learning sucks at some things and excels at some things,” says Joel Johnson, associate professor in the department of earth and planetary sciences at the University of Texas at Austin. Johnson, who was not involved in the TACLS project, knows firsthand the challenges of working with these types of tools. “In general, it’s very easy to have artifacts in your data, false positives. A sensor goes funky, and things like that,” Johnson says. Still, he says TACLS seems “well suited” to the task of predicting flash floods.
False positives do happen, Chandna says. “A real weather system usually affects an area, not just one isolated GNSS station. If one station shows a strong signal but its neighbors do not, that detection can be suppressed. If several nearby stations see the same pattern, we have much more confidence that it represents a real atmospheric signal,” he adds.
Chandna says TACLS is not intended to replace the forecasters who issue weather alerts. It’s just another piece of information that can assist in their decision-making, he says.
Finding a better way
TACLS software is already being used in the LA and San Diego weather forecast offices where flash flooding is a common occurrence, says Laber. “In the West, we deal with a lot more flash flooding, where it happens a lot quicker,” he explains. Today, TACLS shows them a graph with various points telling them what is going on in real time.
A newer version of TACLS with improved graphics is currently being loaded onto the NWS system and is nearly done, Laber says. It will be available to all of the NWS offices in the second half of October, he adds. This iteration has a map with detailed graphics showing how much it’s raining and whether an extreme weather event is occurring.
According to Laber, having more tools — like this latest update to TACLS — will further improve their decision-making when it comes to issuing flash flood alerts, and, in turn, maybe speed up alert times so people know there’s a problem sooner.
Laber says TACLS will likely be used the most in the Western US because the majority of the GNSS sensors are located in places known for earthquake activity. But Chandna thinks TACLS could work well elsewhere too. As long as there are some GNSS sensors and available local weather data, “we could use the same ideology that we have in our system around different parts of the world,” he says.
Small is thinking beyond TACLS. He believes ongoing research is crucial to improving how the NWS issues flash flood warnings. “We learn what’s going on a little more every time we do a storm because they’re all different,” he says. “It’s imperative that you do the research after, especially big events, and see what caused it to do what it did, and why, if it was different than what we already knew, did this occur.”
Lin’s concern is Lanesville and her home. “It would have been helpful to know [water was coming] before I was locked in. I couldn’t go anywhere,” Lin says. “If I got an alert that was like, ‘You need to get out now if you’re in lower-lying ground, this is coming.’ Yeah, that would have [been helpful]. But it came in so fast.”

title: Six Red and White Cooperative outlets completed in Central Papua
content:
Colonel Inf. Fajar Wibawa Angkasa, head of the territorial section at the 173/PVB Regional Military Command, said on Saturday that four of the completed outlets were in Nabire Regency and two in Mimika Regency.
The Indonesian military, or TNI, was tasked with carrying out the physical construction of the KDMP outlets as part of its support for the government program, Angkasa said.
In Nabire, construction is under way at seven locations. Four outlets have been completed, while work at the other three has reached more than 95 percent completion.
In Mimika, construction of the two planned outlets has been completed, he said.
The number of locations could increase, with four potential sites identified in Nabire and three in Mimika, although construction at those sites will depend on whether requirements are met and land is ready, Angkasa said.
According to Angkasa, technical considerations in determining locations include the availability of at least 600 square meters of land and electricity capacity of at least 5,500 watts
Population size is also considered when selecting locations to ensure the cooperatives have a sufficient community base to support their operations.
“Essentially, there is one KDMP in each village. But we first look at the population situation, because there must be at least 500 households. We will prioritize areas with higher population density first,” Angkasa said.
Lieutenant Colonel Arh. Dwi Palwanto Tirta Mentari, commander of the 1705/Nabire Military District Command, said further preparations were needed before the facilities could begin full operations.
Completion of the buildings would not immediately mean full management would be handed over to cooperative administrators, as they would first receive assistance to prepare for operations, he said.
The assistance is planned to cover administrative management, supply chains, sales, and efforts to improve the capacity of cooperative administrators, he added.
Ministry of Cooperatives data shows that a total of 24,701 KDMPs had completed physical development by Sept. 14, with construction still ongoing for 10,866 others.

title: 20年勤めた非正規職員再任用拒み訴訟 市が150万円支払い和解へ

20年勤めた非正規職員再任用拒み訴訟 市が150万円支払い和解へ
福岡県小郡市の非正規職員として約20年勤めた女性（62）が、会計年度任用職員に再任用すると説明されたのに任用を打ち切られたとして、市に550万円の損害賠償を求めて福岡高裁で係争中の国家賠償訴訟が、対応が不適切だったと市が認めて150万円の解決金を支払う内容で和解する見込みになった。市議会が9月18日、関連の議案を全会一致で可決した。
和解案には、解決金の額の口外を禁ずる条項もあるが、議案などから明らかになった。
女性は2002年11月から小郡市の臨時職員や嘱託職員として勤務。会計年度任用職員だった23年3月末に任用を打ち切られた。市側が次年度の勤務先を提示後に撤回した経緯から、一審・福岡地裁久留米支部は今年2月、注意義務違反を一部認め、市に5万5千円の支払いを命じた。双方が控訴したが、福岡高裁は和解を勧告。和解案では、市が解決金を支払うほか、対応が不適切だったことを認め、「遺憾の意を表する」とされた。
18日の市議会で、加地良光市長は「早期かつ円滑な解決を図るため」と和解案受け入れの理由を説明し、「このような誤解を生むような、相互に裁判になるような案件は生み出してはいけないと深く反省している」などと述べた。市の担当部長は解決金について「精神的な苦痛を与えてしまったという性格」と説明し、高裁の裁判官から「少し厳しい判決になる」と言われていた、とも明かした。また、市の担当者と原告の間で認識の共有・確認が足りず、「相手方に一定の不利益を生じさせた点が不適切という点」と説明した。

title: “Entregamos vivienda social nueva que cuesta tres veces menos” que en el mercado”: Brugada
content:
“Entregamos vivienda social nueva que cuesta tres veces menos” que en el mercado”: Brugada
Expuso que su administración ha adquirido “en condiciones de mucha disputa y tensión por el suelo en estos 2 años, 250 mil metros cuadrados para construir vivienda”.
Al participar en la Cumbre de Alcaldes Urban 20 en Nueva York, U20, la jefa de gobierno, Clara Brugada, expresó que su administración está entregando vivienda social nueva que cuesta tres veces menos de lo que vale en el mercado.
Viviendas por menos de 50 mil dólares -860 mil pesos- en zonas donde cuestan ya entre 150 y 200 mil dólares -entre 2 millones 580 mil pesos y 3 millones 440 mil pesos- y en este año arrancamos una empresa pública de construcción de vivienda” dijo en la cumbre en la que participa el alcalde de Nueva York, Zohran Mamdani y el de Barcelona, Jaume Collboni, entre otros.
Brugada expuso que su administración ha adquirido “en condiciones de mucha disputa y tensión por el suelo en estos 2 años, 250 mil metros cuadrados para construir vivienda”.
Se refirió a la estrategia que llevan a cabo a través del Instituto de la Vivienda de la Ciudad de México, INVI, y comentó que entregan créditos a tasa cero a las familias trabajadoras “cuya devolución de este crédito no supera el 20 por ciento de sus ingresos”.
Y expuso que la política de vivienda de su administración es una política de democratización del crédito, de inclusión financiera a quienes históricamente han sido excluidos de la banca tradicional.
Y también se ha incrementado la construcción de vivienda ecológica, dijo la mandataria quien habló de que se han instalado 16 mil sistemas de captación de agua de lluvia, calentadores solares y huertos urbanos.
Y narró que como muchas familias recurren a la autoconstrucción a veces “no tienen techo o tienen grandes problemas porque la familia crece y necesitan la ampliación. Así que mejoramos la habitabilidad de la vivienda para cumplir con el precepto del derecho a una vivienda digna”, hasta el momento se han mejorado 40 mil viviendas que tenían estos problemas.

title: Ohio woman never stopped searching after cat goes missing for 6 years, then viral post reunites them
content:
Six years after her cat disappeared, a Dayton woman found him again when a Humane Society of Greater Dayton post circulated widely, the organization said.
Because the cat arrived at the shelter gravely ill, staff first concentrated on keeping him alive. His connection to a family came to light only afterward.
Here's what to know
After seeing one of the many online shares of the shelter's viral post, a woman suspected the 14-year-old black cat known there as Eugene was actually her missing pet, Booger, as Dayton Daily News reported.
The Humane Society of Greater Dayton (@daytonhumane) said in a Facebook post that it led to a Sept. 11 reunion, six years after he vanished in 2020.
By the time the stray reached the shelter in February 2026, he was in critical condition, suffering from extreme weight loss, dehydration, and significant muscle wasting, according to an Instagram post from the Humane Society of Greater Dayton. He then spent seven months in intensive veterinary treatment, rehabilitation, and recovery care.
Bloodwork showed anemia, and staff also found open wounds, patches of missing fur, ear mites, severe dental disease, and a respiratory infection so serious that he was sneezing blood. Veterinarians said nine teeth had already been lost to dental disease, and they removed nine more.
During his recovery, the cat also tested positive for Feline Immunodeficiency Virus and underwent multiple medicated baths to treat a severe case of ringworm.
More background
The Humane Society of Greater Dayton said it does not know what happened to Booger while he was gone. He survived years away from home before arriving at the shelter in desperate need of extensive care.
"All this time, though, he had a name," the group wrote on Facebook. "He had a history. And he had someone who loved him, missed him and never stopped looking for him."
Over time, vaccinations, medical treatment, and changes to his diet helped him gain weight, regrow his coat, and improve significantly, though the Humane Society of Greater Dayton said the recovery was slow. It also led him to his eventual reunion with his owner.
What can be done?
Keeping photos, veterinary records, and microchip information up to date can make reunions easier when shelters or rescue groups share animals online.
In this cat's case, the Humane Society's posts led the long-lost cat's owner to the realization it might be her furry friend. She was able to back up her suspicions with photos and other personal details.
Upon a reunion at the shelter, the connection was clear. The story gets even better, as an anonymous person waived the adoption fee before the connection was even known.
"Stories like Booger's remind us why we do what we do every single day," said Brian Weltge, president and CEO of the shelter, according to Dayton Daily News. "To see him reunited with the family who never stopped looking for him is an incredible reminder that every animal deserves a chance."
Where can I learn more?
The spirit of this article is alive in other situations where cats are able to reunite in unlikely circumstances, or flourish after a very difficult early life.
• A California cat flew 2,500 miles home to reunite with family in Florida.
• Along a Vietnam highway, a flea-covered cat rescued from trash now lives in Canada.

title: AI reads doctors' notes at scale, revealing data absent from coded medical records
content:
Every time a person sees a doctor, the visit produces two kinds of records. There are the tidy checkbox fields: the billing codes, the lab values, the prescription entries. And there is the note the clinician actually writes, describing what the patient said, how they are coping, what side effects they mentioned and why a medication was changed.
That written note is where most of the medical record lives. It is also where most medical research has never looked.
In a study published today in Nature Medicine, researchers at RespondHealth, co-led with physicians and statisticians at Drexel University and collaborators at Stanford University, the University of Miami, the University of Pennsylvania and the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, describe a system that accurately reads those written notes at scale. It then converts what it finds into data that can be computed and analyzed and keeps every extracted fact linked back to the exact sentence in the chart it came from.
Checking the machine's work
The central question with any AI system reading medical records is whether to believe it. A system that misreads "denies chest pain" as "chest pain" does not just make an error; it manufactures a patient history that never happened.
The researchers built the study around that problem. Board-certified physicians at independent institutions reviewed the system's output line by line against the original notes. One physician reviewed 100 patient visits drawn from 96 different providers and 86 practices across four different electronic health record systems. A second physician independently reviewed a subset of those visits, and a third physician, who did not know which reviewer had said what, settled the disagreements to produce an adjudicated standard.
Measured against that adjudicated standard, the system scored 99.4% on a combined measure of how often it was right about what it reported and how much of what was in the note it caught. The physicians themselves agreed with each other on 94.7% of the statements they both reviewed, which is a reminder that expert judgment has its own variability. The time difference is stark in a different way. The five physician reviewers needed roughly 70 hours to work through 120 charts. The system reviewed each chart in seconds.
To show what the approach makes possible, the team applied it to one of the most widely discussed drug classes in medicine: GLP-1 receptor agonists, the class that includes semaglutide and tirzepatide.
What the researchers found about GLP-1 medications
The team followed more than 16,000 adults who started a GLP-1 medication in routine outpatient care. Some were using the medication to treat diabetes and others for weight loss. The study tracked what happened to them over the following months.
Two patterns stood out, and they ran in opposite directions.
People who started with healthier blood sugar lost more weight and lost it faster. At 12 months, people with normal blood sugar at the start had lost about 7.7% of their body weight, compared with about 2.7% among people whose diabetes was poorly controlled when they began. The time it took to reach 5% weight loss followed the same pattern: about 210 days for people with normal blood sugar and about 413 days for people with poorly controlled diabetes.
Blood sugar improvement went the other way. The people who started with the worst blood sugar control improved the most and improved the fastest. Weight loss also depended on who was taking the medication. At 12 months, women had lost about 6.1% of body weight compared with about 4.0% for men, and adults ages 20 to 39 had lost about 8.1% compared with about 5.1% for those 40 and older.
The researchers stress that this was an observational study of people in ordinary clinical care, not a controlled trial, and that it cannot by itself establish cause and effect. What it can do is show how these medications actually behave outside the tightly managed conditions of a trial.
The part that has been invisible
The study also looked at things that appear almost nowhere in coded medical data because no billing code captures them.
Among patients with a documented baseline, depression scores improved most in those who started out most depressed. In the group with moderate to severe depressive symptoms at the outset, scores fell by about six points on a standard nine-question screening scale over 12 months. Reported pain intensity fell as well, again most clearly among patients who started with the highest pain. Waist circumference declined by about 2.7 inches (6.9 centimeters) over a year in the smaller group of patients for whom it was recorded.
These findings are preliminary and based on modest numbers of patients, and the authors present them as observations worth pursuing rather than conclusions. But they would not have been observable at all without the ability to read clinical notes because these measurements were written down in prose, not entered into a database field.
The same is true of much of the core data. Across the full study population, 70% of the blood sugar readings used in the analysis were found only in written notes. About a third of the evidence that a patient was actually taking a GLP-1 medication came only from notes. Thousands of patients could be included in the analysis only because their starting measurements were recovered from narrative text; using coded fields alone, they would simply have been dropped.
Why it matters
"Most of what a clinician knows about a patient is written in sentences, not stored in fields," said Vicki Seyfert-Margolis, Ph.D., chief executive officer and founder of RespondHealth and a senior author on the study. "For decades we have built evidence about how medicines work in the real world while looking at a fraction of the record. What this work shows is that the rest of it can be made analyzable, and made analyzable in a way that a physician can check."
Charles B. Cairns, M.D., dean of the College of Medicine at Drexel University and a senior author, added, "The point is not that the machine replaces the reviewer. The point is that every number this system produces can be traced back to the sentence in the chart that supports it. A clinician can look at the evidence and disagree. That is what makes it usable in medicine."
The authors note that the method is not specific to GLP-1 medications or diabetes. The same approach can be applied to any condition where the important details are recorded in narrative form, which is to say most of them.

title: Le nombre d’accidents du travail a baissé en 2025
content:
L’association d’assurance accident (AAA) publie ce jeudi son rapport annuel pour l’année 2025 avec une tendance notable : le nombre d’accidents du travail et de trajet sont en baisse par rapport à 2024.
15 295 accidents et maladies professionnelles ont été reconnus par l’association d’assurance accident (AAA) en 2025, selon le rapport annuel publié ce jeudi. Le détail : 12 564 accidents du travail, 2 623 accidents de trajet et 108 maladies professionnelles. Sept accidents mortels ont été enregistrés en 2025, contre cinq en 2024.
En moyenne, l’AAA a reçu 125 déclarations par jour. Le coût moyen d’un accident s’élève à 4 510 euros. Le taux de fréquence continue de baisser : il était de 3,31 % en 2024 et atteint 3 % en 2025, contre 4,54 % en 2019. Quant au nombre d’accidents, celui-ci passe de 6 164 en 2024 à 5 811 en 2025.
Le bâtiment reste le secteur le plus à risque
Le secteur du bâtiment affiche le taux de fréquence le plus élevé avec 7,32 %, suivi de la production alimentaire (6,32 %) et du travail intérimaire (5,86 %).
Les blessures les plus communes sont des plaies et lésions superficielles (53,45 %), des luxations, entorses et foulures (27,53 %) et des fractures osseuses (9,75 %). Elles touchent principalement les membres supérieurs (37,86 %), notamment les mains (27,70 %). Suivent les membres inférieurs (26,43%) où les pieds sont les plus touchés (14,40%). Arrive ensuite le dos (6,09%).
Les accidents surviennent surtout dans des lieux publics (25,88 %), sur des chantiers (22,81 %) et sur des sites industriels (21,09 %). Ils résultent principalement d’écrasements en mouvement (27,15 %), de collisions avec un objet (26,34 %) ou de contact avec un agent matériel coupant ou pointu (16,21 %).
42,01 % de tous les accidents (6 426 sur 15 295) surviennent pendant des «mouvements : marcher, courir, monter, descendre, entrer, sortir, sauter, s’élancer, ramper, grimper, se lever, s’asseoir, nager, plonger». Les gestes du quotidien constituent le premier facteur d’accident.
L’AAA note que le nombre de travailleurs-unité a progressé pour atteindre 505 592 unités, tandis que le nombre d’entreprises a légèrement reculé à 30 988 unités.
La digitalisation s’accélère
L’AAA poursuit sa transformation numérique via Guichet.lu et MyGuichet.lu. Les employeurs peuvent désormais envoyer leurs déclarations d’accidents au format XML, tandis que les assurés consultent en ligne leurs dossiers d’accidents du travail et maladies professionnelles.
«Nous avons poursuivi notre transformation digitale avec le développement des démarches en ligne pour les assurés via MyGuichet.lu. Cette digitalisation vise avant tout à simplifier nos démarches, à faciliter l’accès aux services de l’AAA et à réduire les délais de traitement des dossiers», souligne Georges Wagner, chargé de direction de l’AAA.

title: Australian finalists for Prince William's Earthshot Prize 'nervous but excited'
content:
Indigenous rangers among finalists for Prince William's Earthshot Prize
In short:
An alliance of 70 Indigenous ranger groups who use traditional knowledge to manage Australia's bushfire risks are finalists in Prince William's Earthshot Prize.
They have been recognised for their work to reduce fuel loads and restore biodiversity across the Australian desert.
What's next?
Winners in five categories will be announced in Mumbai on November 17, each taking away a prize worth $1.9 million.
Indigenous rangers responsible for one of the largest cultural burning programs in the world have been named finalists for Prince William's Earthshot Prize.
The prize, which comes with $1.9 million to support each winner's work, aims to reward environmental projects "that will drive significant progress towards repairing the planet".
Samantha Murray, CEO of the Indigenous Desert Alliance (IDA), said she was proud the network of 70 ranger teams across Central Australia had been given global recognition.
"To be recognised on such a massive scale is something that we work really hard at, to make sure that desert rangers are known, they're heard, they're seen."
More than 150 judges selected the IDA from among 7,000 nominations from 169 countries, with Ms Murray admitting she was "slightly nervous, but really excited" about the alliance's prospects.
In the past four years the alliance has engaged 1,300 Indigenous participants, trained 885 rangers and managed fuel loads and restored biodiversity across 145 million hectares of land — an area four times the size of Germany.
Ms Murray, a proud Yilka, Wongutha and Nyoongar woman, said the Right Way Fire program, which combines cultural and Western ways of burning, was key to their nomination for the prize.
The rangers conduct targeted burns to create a mosaic of vegetation which reduces fuel loads, improves native habitats and lessens the risk of large, destructive bushfires.
"Those ways of reading country are when to burn, who to burn by the right people, what times, what weather, what country," Ms Murray said.
She said alliance, formed more than a decade ago, relied on land management practices developed and passed down over tens of thousands of years.
"It really just helped to elevate the way my desert people have been connecting for a very, very long time across different country," she said.
"It's really big about making sure we're continuing that caring for country from our ancestors and our elders, for ourselves and our children."
Prince impressed by 'scale' of IDA's work: CEO
Prince William created the Earthshot Prize in 2020, saying he wanted to reward new ideas and technologies for tackling climate change.
Earthshot Prize CEO Jason Knauf said the prince would be among those who decided who would win in Mumbai in November.
"I think he was absolutely amazed by just the scale [of IDA's work]," he said.
"To have one initiative that is protecting 2.7 million square kilometres — we haven't seen anything like that in the previous six years."
The IDA is one of three finalists in Earthshot's "protect and restore nature" category.
It is up against the Himalayan country Bhutan, which has enshrined environmental protection in its constitution, and the Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative which protects habitats along the Rocky Mountains on the Canada-US border.
Mr Knauf said investing in the knowledge of Indigenous people was key to meeting the global commitment of protecting and conserving 30 per cent of land and sea by 2030.
"Indigenous communities right around the world who are protecting a disproportionate share of the land that we all rely on for our economy … have the deep knowledge about what is going to work in the face of climate change."
If the IDA won, Ms Murray said the funds would boost the alliance's fire protection work, as well as increase the grants available for projects such as trips on country for intergenerational knowledge transfer or ranger exchanges.
She would like to see more desert communities having a "visible presence" in global conversations about climate change.
"We can't ignore the impacts of climate change and how it's impacting and shaping country a little bit differently and making it much harder for desert rangers out there," she said.
'Loudest voice in any room'
Australia has been a strong contender for the prize in the past, with the Indigenous Women Rangers Network in Queensland winning the "revive our oceans" category in 2022.
Local finalists have also included the world's first fully upcycled skyscraper Quay Quarter Tower, the Sydney Institute of Marine Science's living seawalls project, and an Australian-owned cattle and sheep feed supplement which used seaweed.
Mr Knauf said he hoped the recognition would mean the work of the Indigenous Desert Alliance would be shared worldwide.
"We get our whole global network behind them to scale, replicate their work and really champion what they're doing on a global stage," he said.
"We say that we want our finalist to be the loudest voice in any room that they walk into and we help them to achieve that."

title: “Non abbiamo prenotazioni, ma restiamo aperti per la routine dei nostri lavoratori autistici”: l’appello social riempie il ristorante
content:
“Non abbiamo prenotazioni, ma restiamo aperti per la routine dei nostri lavoratori autistici”: l’appello social riempie il ristorante
La ripartenza post-estiva si è rivelata ben più in salita del previsto per il ristorante gourmet Aut&Food di Settimo Milanese, fondato da Matteo Fontana e Leda Pirotta. Arrivati alla serata di lunedì 14 settembre 2026, il libro delle prenotazioni segnava un inesorabile zero. Piuttosto che abbassare la serranda e spezzare la fondamentale regolarità settimanale dei cinque dipendenti autistici – Riccardo, Fabrizio, Zaira, Davide e Simone, di età compresa tra i 22 e i 31 anni –, il titolare ha scelto la via della trasparenza affidandosi ai social media. In un post ha scritto:
Questo lunedì non abbiamo prenotazioni al ristorante, ma non rimarremo chiusi perché abbiamo assunto regolarmente ragazzi che hanno più necessità di altri di mantenere la loro routine settimanale.
Quel che Fontana non si aspettava era che quelle parole scritte sulla pagina Facebook del locale dessero il via a una straordinaria ondata di condivisioni e solidarietà collettiva.
Dal rischio della sala vuota al tutto esaurito grazie alla solidarietà
Nel giro di poche ore il messaggio ha fatto il giro della rete, trasformando una serata a rischio in un successo inatteso che ha portato 52 prenotazioni, sfiorando la capienza massima di 70 posti del locale ricavato all’interno di un antico cascinale. L’entusiasmo dei giovani lavoratori è esploso di fronte all’improvviso arrivo dei clienti con i ragazzi che si sono subito dati da fare, contentissimi che il ristorante fosse così pieno.
Inclusione, accoglienza e menù gourmet per un progetto unico sul territorio
Un traguardo straordinario per un progetto nato dall’associazione dei due fondatori, fortemente motivati dal futuro del figlio di 9 anni con autismo severo e ispirati dall’esperienza di PizzAut. Dietro il successo della serata c’è infatti un percorso di inclusione laboriosa e attenta, che ha permesso a ragazzi alla loro prima esperienza o reduci da lunghi tirocini di ottenere le abilitazioni professionali per lavorare in cucina e in sala.
Per agevolare la loro autonomia, i tavoli sono dotati di speciali tovagliette geometriche che guidano nell’ordinato posizionamento delle posate, dei bicchieri e del calice da vino, mentre l’architettura rustica del cascinale viene protetta dal baccano grazie al civismo dei clienti. L’offerta gastronomica spazia da un menù fisso fino alla recente introduzione della formula informale con Aut-Burger e pinsa.
Ti potrebbe interessare anche:
- PizzAut sarà la pizzeria ufficiale del Gran Premio di Monza di Formula 1 (e quest’anno ci sarà la pizza dedicata a Kimi Antonelli)
- PizzAut fa la storia! Alla IULM di Milano nasce il primo ristorante universitario al mondo gestito da ragazzi con autismo
- Simone, ragazzo autistico ed ex cameriere di PizzAut, si è laureato in Economia e lavora per una multinazionale (ma continua a fare il volontario)

일본에서 지역 우체국을 의료 거점으로 활용하는 움직임이 확산하고 있다. 인구 감소와 고령화로 병·의원이 사라지는 지역이 늘자 전국 곳곳에 마련된 우체국 공간을 활용해 의사가 순회 진료를 돌고 온라인으로 사후 관리하는 방식이다.
23일 니혼게이자이신문에 따르면 야마구치현 슈난시는 2024년 7월 일본에서 처음으로 우체국에 순회진료소를 설치했다. 산간지역인 와다지구의 다카세우체국에 마련된 진료소에서 매주 화요일 대면 진료와 온라인 진료를 번갈아 실시한다. 의사는 다카세우체국에서 20㎞ 정도 떨어진 병원에서 온다.
와다지구에서 종합병원까지는 자동차로 약 30분 걸린다. 온라인 진료 때는 간호사가 환자 곁에서 진료를 돕는다. 겨울철 도로 통제와 태풍 등으로 이동이 어려운 상황에서도 의료 서비스를 제공할 수 있다는 것이 장점으로 꼽힌다.
일본 전국에 약 2만4000곳이 있는 우체국은 지역 주민에게 익숙하고 접근성이 높다는 점에서 의료 거점으로 주목받는다. 환자는 우체국에서 진료비를 내고 처방약을 우편으로 받을 수 있다.
다른 지방자치단체도 비슷한 움직임에 나섰다. 미에현 도바시의 도서지역 도시아지마에서는 지난해 10월부터 우체국 온라인 진료 실증 사업을 하고 있다. 홋카이도 오무초는 올해 우체국 두 곳에 온라인 진료를 정식 도입했다. 진료 과목을 내과, 외과 중심에서 안과로 확대하는 방안을 검토하고 있다.
배경에는 의료 공백 심화가 있다. 일본 후생노동성에 따르면 주변에 의료기관이 없는 지역은 2025년 10월 말 기준 전국 575곳으로 2022년보다 18곳 늘었다.
일본 정부도 제도를 정비하고 있다. 올해 4월 시행된 의료법을 통해 온라인 진료가 법제화됐다. 이를 바탕으로 후생노동성은 의료 제공 체계를 지원할 방침이다. 다만 전문가들은 우체국 온라인 진료가 의료 접근성을 높일 수 있지만 대면 진료를 완전히 대체할 수는 없다고 지적한다. 간호사뿐 아니라 임상검사기사와 물리치료사 등 다양한 의료 인력이 참여하도록 하고, 온라인과 대면 진료를 적절히 결합하는 방식이 필요하다고 주장한다.

title: 20代で大けが、絶望から「ばあちゃんビジネス」へ 創業者の恩返し
content:
20代で大けが、絶望から「ばあちゃんビジネス」へ 創業者の恩返し
75歳以上の高齢者に生きがいと、収入、居場所を。そんな目標を掲げ、働く場を生み出してきた人がいます。「うきはの宝」代表取締役の大熊充さん（46）。「ばあちゃんビジネス」を手がけるきっかけは、20代のときに生死をさまよったバイク事故でした。
バイク事故で車いすに 「もう僕は、終わった」
台所では、「ばあちゃん」たちがリズム良く食材を刻んでいた。お盆に、熱々のエビチリや中華スープ、炊き込みご飯など野菜たっぷりの料理が並ぶ。
週1回、3時間半だけ営業する「ばあちゃん喫茶 春日ぶどうの庭店」（福岡県春日市）。客の「おいしい」に、ばあちゃんたちの顔がほころんだ。
福岡県うきは市出身の大熊さん。
先生と折り合いが悪く、中学で不登校に。
高校は入学後すぐやめた。
大阪へ行きバイク屋を目指すも、椎間板（ついかんばん）ヘルニアで夢破れた。
転機は、25歳の夜だった。
宮崎県内をバイクで走っていたら、カーブで石に乗り上げ中央分離帯に激突。鎖骨を粉砕骨折し、けがの手術から別の病気を発症した。右半身が動かず、車いすになった。
「もう僕は、終わった」
不眠症になり心が安定せず、入院中は夜になると、転倒のおそれがある高齢者とともにナースステーションの近くに集められた。そんな自分に、話しかけてくる人たちがいた。
「どこが悪いん？」
「何で入院しとるん？」
ばあちゃんたちは、自分が一番聞かれたくないことを遠慮なく尋ねてくる。
うっとうしくて、無視した。
それでも毎晩、声をかけてきた。
うるさいほど元気だったばあちゃんが…
だんだん可笑（おか）しくな…

title: British Sikh man granted bail in India nine years after arrest
content:
Jagtar Singh Johal, a British Sikh man who was arrested in India in 2017 in connection with alleged terrorism offences, has been granted bail by a Delhi court.
Johal, from Scotland, was arrested for his alleged role in funding the Khalistan Liberation Force, which had carried out targeted killings in India’s Punjab region.
His full trial has been repeatedly deferred by the authorities in the federal court but largely similar conspiracy charges were dismissed by a court in Punjab last year. Throughout his detention the prosecution has failed to produce verifiable evidence, leading to the deferred hearings.
Johal, now 39, travelled to India to marry his fiancee in late 2017. On 4 November, three weeks after the wedding, the couple were shopping with a relative in the Punjab city of Jalandhar when a group of men took Johal from his car, placed a black hood over his head and put him in an unmarked vehicle. He claims he was then denied access to a lawyer and tortured in an attempt to extract a confession. A question remains over whether he was arrested following a tip-off from British intelligence services.
Commenting on Friday’s ruling, Johal’s Scotland-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “The past two years has been an expensive rollercoaster, contesting bails at the supreme court and back to the high court. I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison. We have waited so long and fought so hard for this moment.”
He added of previous hearings: “Whenever the evidence against Jagtar is tested in court, judges find what we’ve said all along, which is that there isn’t any.
“How long will this sick joke of a legal process be allowed to continue? We’re obviously delighted that Jagtar will soon be released, but he won’t be truly free until he is back in Dumbarton, with his wife and family.”
Gurpreet Johal, who also lives in Dumbarton, has lobbied a succession of UK foreign secretaries, who have repeatedly admitted the case has dragged on too long, but have been reluctant to call publicly for his release on the grounds that they should not interfere in the judiciary of another country.
The UK government recently appointed Alistair Burt as a special envoy for complex consular cases and he has met Gurpreet Johal in Scotland to discuss the case.
Dan Dolan, the deputy executive director of Reprieve, one of the organisation’s fighting for Johal’s release, said: “While this judgment is welcome as Jagtar should not be in prison a day longer, we must now watch closely to ensure this order is actually implemented and not obstructed in any way. The conditions attached are likely to be onerous. We must also remember that Jagtar will still be facing the death penalty in eight cases against him, despite these cases essentially duplicating trumped-up charges on which he has already been fully acquitted.”
Chris Esdaile, a senior legal adviser to Redress, another organisaiton representing Johal, said granting bail “can’t undo the intolerable suffering caused by nine years of arbitrary detention”.
He added: “The need for accountability for the allegations of torture and the deeply flawed proceedings against Jagtar remains urgent.”
Johal’s lawyers said they were still awaiting the details of what would happen next in relation to posting bail terms. While the judges’ order was that Jagtar should be released on bail, he remained in custody while judges confirmed his bail conditions, which may be stringent. The court must also confirm the sums of money that must be posted as a bond.

title: SP u džudu za veterane: Prva medalja za BiH, Evropljanima svih 18 zlata
content:
SP u džudu za veterane: Prva medalja za BiH, Evropljanima svih 18 zlata
Današnji dan donio je i veliko slavlje za domaću publiku jer je Bosna i Hercegovina stigla do prve medalje na ovom takmičenju. Bosnu i Hercegovinu danas je predstavljalo devet takmičara: Hasan Mehić, Avdo Bešić, Zijad Sejdinović, Milanko Mučibabić, Nikola Kljajić, Arif Libić, Elvir Salihagić, Zikret Hasanica i Dragan Božović.
Junak dana za našu reprezentaciju bio je Mučibabić, koji je u kategoriji veterana M9 do 100 kilograma osvojio srebrnu medalju. Na putu do finala Mučibabić je bio bolji od rivala iz Francuske, Velike Britanije i Rusije, dok mu je najsjajnije odličje izmaklo porazom od reprezentativca Kube Luisa Torresa Cobasa.
Finalne borbe ponudile su vrhunski džudo, a dominantnu ulogu imali su evropski takmičari kojima su pripale sve zlatne medalje današnjeg programa.
Najuspješnija je bila Njemačka sa tri osvojena zlata, dok su po dvije zlatne medalje izborili predstavnici Austrije, Rusije, Rumunije i Francuske. Po jedno najsjajnije odličje otišlo je u Moldaviju, Brazil, Hrvatsku, Španiju, Češku, Švedsku i Nizozemsku.
Nakon četvrtog takmičarskog dana došlo je i do promjena na vrhu tabelarnog poretka. Gruzija je zadržala vodeću poziciju sa devet zlatnih medalja, na drugo mjesto se probila Francuska sa sedam, dok je treća Rusija sa šest. Po pet zlatnih odličja u dosadašnjem toku takmičenja sakupili su Brazil i Kazahstan.
Podsjećamo, ovo jedno od najmasovnijih takmičenja u organizaciji Džudo saveza Bosne i Hercegovine okuplja 1.350 takmičara iz 65 zemalja.
Nakon završetka veteranskih borbi, vikend u Areni Hills rezervisan je za takmičenje u katama i Specijalnu olimpijadu, a ulaz za sve ljubitelje džuda i dalje je besplatan.

title: Bulgaria's battery storage boom pays off as summer drought hits power plants
content:
Low administrative hurdles, a receptive market for clean energy and EU funding are among the reasons expert cite for the country's leading green energy role in the region.
As Eastern Europe's power sector has taken a hit from a record drought, Bulgaria has benefitted from building out battery storage capacity alongside its rapid solar expansion.
Around a hundred battery energy storage system (BESS) sites are now operating, most of them built in the past two years.
The large-scale projects take advantage of former industrial sites and airfields or are integrated into existing power stations, including coal-fired plants.
"The scale and speed of storage deployment in Bulgaria is unprecedented in a European context," Stavros Papathanassiou, a professor at the National Technical University of Athens, told the AFP news agency.
Low administrative hurdles, a receptive market for clean energy and EU funding are among the reasons expert cite for the country's leading role in the region.
The battery installations absorb surplus power from solar installations and feed it back into the grid when demand rises.
That proved a boon when exceptionally low levels on the River Danube disrupted power generation at nuclear and hydroelectric plants in Eastern Europe, boosting demand for electricity imports.
In July and August, Bulgaria, one of the EU's poorest countries, recorded net electricity exports of around 830 gigawatt-hours a month, more than twice the average in May and June.
In July alone, Romania accounted for nearly half of Bulgaria's outward electricity transfers, valued at an estimated €74 million.
Reducing coal reliance
At Maritsa East 3, once Bulgaria's second-largest coal-fired power plant, the shift away from dependence on the fuel is visible on the ground.
Built under communism with four generating units, the plant sharply reduced coal operations in 2024, repurposing existing grid infrastructure for a battery facility.
"We could leverage the large connection to the grid. We decided to disconnect one coal unit and connect batteries," said Vassil Shtonov, head of Bulgaria operations for the British-based power company ContourGlobal.
"Coal is out, battery is in. It was the right place at the right time," Shtonov told AFP, though he said Bulgaria should maintain a minimum coal-fired reserve for severe winters or disruptions to gas supplies.
While Bulgaria accounted for about 9% of European battery-storage additions and about 2% of solar additions in 2025, it can "serve as a positive example for other European nations," said Lennart Herrmann at the Munich-based research and consulting firm FfE.
"The right incentives...can enable a swift energy transition," he told AFP.
The Bulgarian energy ministry said the country had around 5.7 gigawatts of operational battery-storage power capacity this month.
That is equivalent, in power terms, to nearly a quarter of Bulgaria's installed power-generation capacity overall and more than five times neighbouring Romania's operational battery capacity.
Businesses in Bulgaria have also signed contracts for nearly 14 gigawatt-hours of large‑scale storage, part of which has already come online.
"The aim is for storage systems to find a sustainable role in the market," the ministry said, adding that it "must go hand in hand with other investments, such as in transmission and distribution grids."
'By chance'
Nikola Gazdov, president of Bulgaria's Association for Production, Storage and Trading of Electricity, attributed the battery boom to a combination of factors rather than a crafted strategy.
"Everything happened almost by chance," he told AFP.
Solar and wind capacity has expanded rapidly across the region, but Bulgaria's renewables boom has been particularly solar-heavy, creating growing daytime surpluses.
And in Bulgaria, large battery projects can be up and running in just nine to 18 months, much less than many solar or wind projects, Gazdov added.
But battery storage technology has its limits.
One is that grid connections with neighbouring countries are limited in the amount of current they can transport.
Another is that current batteries can store power only for relatively short periods, "typically between one and six, sometimes up to eight hours," said Herrmann at FfE.
So while they can support the grid in case of a temporary drop in power supply, they cannot replace a nuclear reactor that goes offline due to drought.
And their success could ultimately reduce their own profitability, because when more BESS operators buy electricity when prices are low and sell it back at peak times, the gap between the two price periods will narrow.

title: Ethiopia’s Wheat Revolution Delivers a Powerful Message: Africa Can Feed Itself — President Taye
content:
Ethiopia’s Wheat Revolution Delivers a Powerful Message: Africa Can Feed Itself — President Taye
Addis Ababa, September 24, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia’s transformation from a wheat-importing country into one of Africa’s largest wheat producers is demonstrating the continent’s capacity to strengthen its own food security, President Taye Atske-Selassie told the 81st United Nations General Assembly.
Addressing the General Assembly in New York, President Taye highlighted Ethiopia’s rapid progress in wheat production, supported by the introduction and expansion of climate-resilient wheat varieties.
He presented the transformation against a backdrop of growing pressure on global food systems, where access to food has increasingly become a strategic concern and disruptions to supply chains can have consequences far beyond national borders.
“At a time where food provision has become a political battleground and the global food supply hangs precariously in the balance, we send a clear message that Africa can feed itself,” President Taye said.
Ethiopia’s experience, he noted, demonstrates the potential for African countries to harness their agricultural resources, expand domestic production and strengthen resilience against external food-supply pressures.
The transformation from importer to major producer also reflects Ethiopia’s broader emphasis on building productive capacity as a foundation for sustainable development. By expanding climate-resilient agricultural production, the country is seeking to strengthen food availability while contributing to wider economic resilience.
President Taye’s remarks place Ethiopia’s wheat gains within a broader continental context: Africa’s large agricultural potential can be translated into greater food production when supported by appropriate technologies, investment and climate-resilient approaches.
The President linked food security with Ethiopia’s wider development priorities, including renewable energy, connectivity, manufacturing and urban development, while calling for genuine and sustained regional and international cooperation to sustain and scale up these gains.
Ethiopia’s wheat transformation, therefore, was presented at the UNGA not simply as a national agricultural achievement, but as evidence of the capacity for African countries to build stronger, more resilient food systems and advance toward greater food self-reliance.

title: Governo garante que 97% dos pedidos do Creche Feliz têm vaga atribuída
content:
Governo garante que 97% dos pedidos do Creche Feliz têm vaga atribuída
A capacidade instalada no programa Creche Feliz ultrapassa atualmente as 141 mil crianças, tendo o Governo avançado este ano com uma plataforma centralizada para gestão e procura das vagas.
A ministra do Trabalho, Solidariedade e Segurança Social afirmou esta sexta-feira que 97% dos pedidos do programa Creche Feliz têm vaga atribuída, avançando que desde abril de 2024 foram criadas mais de 19 mil vagas gratuitas.

“Neste momento, 97% dos pedidos à escala nacional têm vaga atribuída”, afirmou Rosário Palma Ramalho, acrescentando que, desde abril de 2024, foram criadas mais de 19 mil vagas gratuitas.
A governante falava em Bugalhos, no concelho de Alcanena, distrito de Santarém, na primeira de três inaugurações realizadas esta sexta-feira, que abrangeram também Monsanto e Minde e acrescentam 155 lugares à rede local de creches.
Segundo a ministra, a capacidade instalada no programa Creche Feliz ultrapassa atualmente as 141 mil crianças, tendo o Governo avançado este ano com uma plataforma centralizada para gestão e procura das vagas.
A ministra destacou também a atualização das comparticipações pagas pelo Estado, que aumentaram 8,7% em 2025 e 6,9% em 2026, afirmando que o objetivo é assegurar o pagamento integral do custo das vagas gratuitas.
A subida de 6,9% em 2026 elevou a comparticipação mensal por vaga em creche de 515,90 para 551,50 euros, segundo informação divulgada pelo Governo.
Rosário Palma Ramalho disse ainda que foram cumpridas “por completo” as metas previstas no Plano de Recuperação e Resiliência (PRR) para esta resposta social, depois de um “grande impulso” dado pelo programa.
“Para o futuro teremos que recorrer a outros instrumentos de financiamento, que também serão disponibilizados, com suporte às necessidades que vão fazer-se sentir nos vários concelhos”, afirmou aos jornalistas.
O Governo anunciou no início de setembro que as metas do PRR sob responsabilidade do Ministério do Trabalho, Solidariedade e Segurança Social foram cumpridas, contabilizando 7.543 lugares de creche criados ou remodelados através daquele plano.
Em Alcanena, as duas novas creches municipais de Bugalhos e Monsanto e a ampliação da resposta do Centro de Bem Estar Social de Minde representam um investimento global de cerca de 3,4 milhões de euros e fazem aumentar de 150 para 305 a capacidade do concelho.
“É importantíssimo nós termos estes equipamentos porque combate o nosso envelhecimento demográfico, apoia as famílias” e constitui também um suporte para o desenvolvimento empresarial, afirmou a ministra.
Rosário Palma Ramalho salientou que o crescimento empresarial e industrial da região exige respostas para os trabalhadores e defendeu que o Estado deve funcionar como “parceiro das famílias”, em articulação com as autarquias e o setor social e solidário.
A governante considerou ainda que as respostas devem ser adaptadas a cada território, afirmando que são as autarquias que melhor identificam as necessidades locais e que cabe depois à administração central avaliar e apoiar os projetos.
O presidente da Câmara de Alcanena, Rui Anastácio, destacou que o município “mais do que duplicou” em pouco mais de dois anos as vagas de creche e afirmou que está também a multiplicar por quatro a oferta pública de habitação.
O autarca enquadrou os investimentos numa estratégia destinada a criar condições para a permanência ou regresso de jovens e famílias ao concelho, conjugando respostas sociais, habitação e desenvolvimento empresarial.
As novas respostas disponibilizam 56 lugares em Bugalhos, 61 em Monsanto e mais 38 em Minde, elevando para 305 o número total de vagas de creche no concelho.
As creches de Bugalhos e Monsanto resultam da reconversão de antigas escolas primárias entretanto encerradas, com Rui Anastácio a salientar que o município está agora a “reabrir duas escolas fechadas” para voltar a acolher crianças.
A ministra defendeu ainda que a creche deve ser encarada também como uma resposta educativa, salientando que é nos primeiros mil dias de vida que podem começar as desigualdades sociais e que estas estruturas contribuem para a integração das crianças desde a primeira infância.

title: Panatta: “Tre giorni di vero tennis”, scudetto U14 femminile al Club La Meridiana
content:
Il Club La Meridiana è il nuovo campione d’Italia Under 14 femminile a squadre. Nella finale disputata oggi all’Adriano Panatta Racquet Club di Treviso, la formazione emiliana ha superato con un netto 2-0 la Canottieri Casale, conquistando lo scudetto al termine di tre intense giornate di gare che hanno riunito le otto migliori squadre italiane della categoria.
Per il club emiliano si tratta del coronamento di un percorso iniziato nelle fasi provinciali e regionali e proseguito attraverso i tabelloni di macroarea fino alla fase finale nazionale. Alle spalle delle vincitrici si è classificata la Canottieri Casale, mentre il terzo posto è andato al Tc Santa Margherita davanti al Club Nautico. A completare la graduatoria il Tc Cagliari, il Tc Parioli, il Tc Rungg Bolzano e il Tc Diamante.
L’edizione 2026 dei Campionati italiani Under 14 femminili ha segnato anche il debutto dell’Adriano Panatta Racquet Club nell’organizzazione di una fase nazionale della competizione. Per la prima volta Treviso ha ospitato l’evento, accogliendo oltre quaranta tra atlete e tecnici provenienti da tutta Italia, oltre a dirigenti, accompagnatori e addetti ai lavori.
Inaugurato nel 2021, il centro sportivo trevigiano si estende su oltre due ettari e dispone di sei campi da tennis, sei campi da padel, palestra, piscina, area wellness e club house. Strutture e servizi che hanno consentito di ospitare al meglio una manifestazione nazionale, garantendo condizioni ottimali per atlete e staff nel corso dell’intero torneo.
Le sfide sono state trasmesse in diretta televisiva e sull’app di SuperTennis, richiamando numerosi appassionati sugli spalti del circolo. Tra i presenti anche Adriano Panatta, che ha seguito da vicino gli incontri e l’evoluzione della competizione.
“Siamo orgogliosi di aver ospitato un evento così bello, nel quale per tre giorni si è respirato e vissuto il vero tennis. Abbiamo visto all’opera diverse squadre con giocatrici di talento, non solo dal punto di vista tecnico, ma anche per personalità e carattere», ha dichiarato Panatta. «Se la manifestazione è riuscita così bene, il merito è del lavoro di squadra fatto insieme al Comune di Treviso e alla Federazione. Complimenti al Club La Meridiana per la vittoria e un grande in bocca al lupo per il futuro”.

title: Million Moves: Perth swimmer Kate Wallington with autism leads AusActive’s campaign to get Aussies moving
content:
Kate Wallington is a champion swimmer. Ever since she started swimming at age eight, she feels most at peace gliding through the water even in the face of intense competition and pressure.
She was also diagnosed with autism at age 16, and with ADHD two years later.
A lack of diagnoses as a kid meant Ms Wallington had a “rough” experience in childhood: a combination of isolation from her peers and being misunderstood by teachers led to a swathe of mental health problems.
“I was very misunderstood by the school system, which I think a lot of people are. . .It was really hard to fit in as someone who was swimming nine times a week plus gym sessions,” Ms Wallington described.
“(I was an) insane perfectionist. . . that led to some insane burnout because I just had to be the best at everything.”
The pile-on of mental health, social, and education problems — on top of several hostile experiences from swim clubs and coaches —also resulted in an epilepsy diagnosis for the champion swimmer.
It’s little wonder Ms Wallington feels most at peace in the pool. It’s a quieting, calm environment where she could escape from how life was treating her on land well into her adulthood.
“It’s just so regulating. . . it just feels right to be in the water,” she said.
“When I race, when I’m at competitions, and when I’m training, the world doesn’t exist anymore.”
It’s telling: the 20-year-old holds 14 world records, five Australian records, and a total of 11 gold medals at the 2025 Virtus World Swimming Championships.
“That was just my absolute, lifelong childhood dream. . . walking out onto the pool deck in like the green and gold, because from eight years old, I decided that I was going to represent Australia,” she said.
Ms Wallington, who is studying sports science and exercise physiology, has been taking part in AusActive’s Million Moves campaign, which aims to help Aussies create healthy habits through regular movement and exercise for free.
Ms Wallington has been leading up the Murdoch University gym’s Million Moves effort to notch up one million moves (one minute of movement = one move) between September 1 and 21.
AusActive WA general manager Karinda Lobb says a key aspect of Million Moves is to help lower the barrier of accessibility to exercise and a healthy lifestyle to Australians who might be limited by time or money.
It’s also an effort to divert people away from Australia’s already creaking health system, which Ms Lobb says spends “millions of dollars” on diseases that “could be prevented”.
“We all work together to take pressure off, you know, the hospitals and and and the system, but also get more people to understand that moving can be simple and it doesn’t have to involve a lot, and it can be at any level,” Ms Lobb said.
Through her job as a support worker, Ms Wallington has come to realise that movement for her clients — many of whom have similar diagnoses to her — was providing a space for them to regulate in a way her swimming was doing for her.
“It’s not just that I love swimming, I love competing and that I want to win and go to the Olympics. . . I genuinely need this for my everyday,” she said.
“If there was no competition at all, I would still be doing this. I would still be moving.”
In spite of her tough lot in life, Ms Wallington has found a community in both swimming and the gym, and has encouraged other Australians to find their own routines even if they’re hesitant.
“I promise you, there’s a space for everyone in sport or in exercise, and even if you haven’t found it yet, you will,” she said.

More information about AusActive’s free Million Moves campaign is available at millionmoves.org.au.
